doc.title: Joe Bushkin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Recording with Billie Holiday and Bernie Hanighen; publishers' practices
summary: 1936 sessions with Billie Holiday arranged by Bernie Hanighen, and how music publishers worked.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Let me ask you about a couple of recordings. And if my information is correct, in 1936 you recorded with Billie Holiday.
Yeah. “Billie’s Blues,” “Summertime,” and, yeah, that became a classic 78.
She was just — well where was her career at that point? Was she well known?

No she was singing and carrying on in a saloon up in Harlem, as one of the young, good looking, black gals that the audience would dig. And Bernie Hanighen, who wrote “As Long as I Live” and a bunch of other good tunes with Johnny Mercer, was a big fan of Bunny Berigan’s, Artie Shaw, myself included. And he’s the one, he was an A&R man, a Repertoire Artists Director of Vocalion Records. And not John Hammond, but Bernie Hanighen was the first guy to record Billie Holiday. And I went down to Bernie’s little pad in Greenwich Village. I had a whole stack of lead sheets from motion picture themes and various songs that the publishers were publishing at the time. That whole business has done a complete 180 turn, where The Beatles, I must give them credit for the fact that they published their own music. Because once they made a hit, no one else was going to make it. But that’s not what went on in the music business at the time. They had the Jimmy Dorsey Band, Woody Herman, Benny Goodman, you know all of the different bands who were recording for various companies, and that was the reason to have a publisher but I must say, like all mortgage brokers and bankers, they had fifty percent of © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-
the action. Whereas the lyricist got twenty-five percent and the composer got twenty-five percent.
So the publishers were making out pretty well.
Oh they were doing great. And they had some very low paying professional men running around delivering lead sheets.
Trying to get the bands to record their songs.
Yeah right. And then the publishers might come up with a case of scotch or some, you know, whatever you want to call it I guess, a payola, of that time.
